table.ruleA: 6 forms, form 1 at hopper; volume/upper/lower marks 10/7/3, 8/6/2, 12/9/4, 6/5/2, 9/7/3, 7/5/2; start 3,6,6,2,2,1; all GREEN; waste tally 0; line limit 38; halves and quarters rounded down
table.ruleB: 6 tanks, tank 1 at inlet; same volumes, marks, starting contents; all STEADY; outfall total 0; train limit 38; halves and quarters rounded down
table.difference: Only the names differ: GREEN=STEADY, HOT=OVERLOADED, waste tally=outfall total, washout=storm bypass. The charge table and the inflow schedule are identical.

table.ruleA: Add this cycle's charge to every form. Volume is not enforced.
table.ruleB: Add this cycle's inflow to every tank. Volume is not enforced.

table.ruleA: Forms handled in order 1 to 6. If contents are strictly above volume, the excess goes to form n+1 before that form is handled (so it can cascade), and the form is set to its volume. Excess from form 6 goes to waste.
table.ruleB: Tanks handled in order 1 to 6. If contents are strictly above volume, the excess goes to tank n+1 before that tank is handled (so it can cascade), and the tank is set to its volume. Excess from tank 6 goes to outfall.

table.ruleA: States are read after Step 2. GREEN with contents >= upper mark becomes HOT. HOT with contents <= lower mark becomes GREEN. Otherwise no change. At most one change per cycle. Each change is logged as (cycle, form, before, after).
table.ruleB: States are read after Step 2. STEADY with contents >= upper mark becomes OVERLOADED. OVERLOADED with contents <= lower mark becomes STEADY. Otherwise no change. At most one change per cycle. Each change is logged as (cycle, tank, before, after).

table.ruleA: All six amounts are computed first, from contents at the start of the step: GREEN gives floor(contents/4), HOT gives floor(contents/2). Then all are applied at once. Each form loses its amount. A GREEN amount goes to waste. A HOT amount goes to form n-1, or to waste if the form is 1. Volume is not enforced.
table.ruleB: Tanks handled one at a time in order 1 to 6, each applied before the next. The amount is computed from the tank's contents when it is reached: STEADY gives floor(contents/4), OVERLOADED gives floor(contents/2). The tank loses its amount. A STEADY amount goes to outfall. An OVERLOADED amount goes to tank n-1, or to outfall if the tank is 1. Volume is not enforced.
table.difference: The wording differs (simultaneous in A, sequential in B) but the function is the same. In B the only transfer goes up the line to n-1, and that tank has always been handled already. So when B reaches a tank, its contents are still exactly its contents at the start of the step, and its amount equals A's. The returned liquor lands after the receiving tank's amount is already taken, which is what A's 'compute all, then apply' does. If B's order were 6 to 1, the results would differ.

table.ruleA: Sum all six forms. If the total is strictly above 38 (equal to 38 does not fire), every form becomes floor(contents/2), all six forms included. All removed units go to waste, and the cycle is recorded.
table.ruleB: Sum all six tanks. If the total is strictly above 38 (equal to 38 does not fire), every tank becomes floor(contents/2), all six tanks included. All removed liquor goes to outfall, and the cycle is logged.

table.ruleA: At the end of cycle 5, after Step 5: (a) end mix for forms 1 to 6, (b) end statuses, (c) all status changes, (d) washout cycles, (e) waste tally, (f) balance check: start total + charges = end total + waste.
table.ruleB: At the end of cycle 5, after Step 5: (a) end contents for tanks 1 to 6, (b) end states, (c) all state changes, (d) storm bypass cycles, (e) outfall total, (f) balance check: start total + inflows = end total + outfall, with both sides shown.
table.difference: B also asks for both sides of the balance check to be shown. That is a presentation detail and does not change any result.

result.probeWhy: The only real wording difference is Step 4: A computes everything at once, B goes one tank at a time. The probe sends large charges to every position in cycle 1, so all six positions go HOT/OVERLOADED together and each one returns liquor to its neighbour up the line in the same Step 4. If B's sequential order ever let returned liquor reach a tank before that tank's own amount was taken, the results would split. The probe also fires the halving in four cycles and drives several HOT-to-GREEN-to-HOT flips through cycles 4 and 5. To check that the probe can detect an order problem, I ran a deliberately wrong version with B's order reversed (6 to 1). That version differs on the probe (end 4,3,4,3,3,2, halvings in cycles 1,3,5, loss 155) and on the printed tables. The real B never differs.
result.differingRule: None. The only real wording difference is Step 4 (A computes all amounts first, B handles tanks one by one from 1 to 6), and it is the same in function: the only transfer goes back up the line to a tank already handled.
result.trust: Both routes agree. The table explains why the Step 4 wording difference does not matter, and the probe confirms it. As an extra check, I ran both procedures on 200,000 random starting and input tables (values 0 to 9) and found 0 differences. The reversed-order version differed on 199,968 of them, so the comparison does catch an order bug. The balance check holds in every run (printed: 20 start + 109 inputs = 38 end + 76 waste). Scripts are at C:\Users\USER\AppData\Local\Temp\om\desk-fm\P06\p06_claude_check.py. Another process was writing to the same folder at the same time: it replaced my first script, sim.py, with its own version halfway through. I left that file alone, did the final runs in my own uniquely named file, and the results matched my first run exactly.

differing_rule_reported: None. The only real wording difference is Step 4 (A computes all amounts first, B handles tanks one by one from 1 to 6), and it is the same in function: the only transfer goes back up the line to a tank already handled.
